content.text:
Some of minecraft's settings are not stored in any config file on this server — they are read from the environment when the game starts, and the only place an instance can set them is .grizzly/env, at the top of the data directory. It is always there, often empty. Don't go looking for a config file for these: there isn't one, and searching for it is time spent on something that cannot be found.

Exactly these settings do anything in that file, and the rest are ignored: TYPE, VERSION, MEMORY, MODRINTH_PROJECTS, MODRINTH_DOWNLOAD_DEPENDENCIES and MODRINTH_PROJECTS_DEFAULT_VERSION_TYPE. A line naming anything else is dropped when the game launches, so the change will look like it worked and won't have.

Read the file first to see what's already set, then change it like any other config file — one setting at a time — and restart to apply it. That restart self-guards: if the game refuses a value and won't start, the previous version of the file is restored and the server restarted automatically, and you'll be told. So a value you're unsure of is worth trying rather than talking around; afterwards, read_logs to confirm it took rather than assuming.

Here is how mods work on minecraft. These rules are specific to this game — another game's identifiers and install steps are different, so ask for its guide separately rather than reusing this one.

Minecraft servers can also take mods and datapacks, and it's the one game here where you can install them. Never name a mod or datapack from memory: slugs get renamed, and a slug that doesn't exist stops the server from starting — and because the bad value is read back off the same disk, a replacement server fails the same way, so that is the one break that can't be undone for you. Use search_mods to find candidates, then mod_info to confirm the exact slug exists and supports both the loader and the Minecraft version that server actually runs. Prefer datapacks and mods that work server-side: they cost the players nothing. When a project is also required on the client, say so before you install it — every player would have to install that file, and the loader, on their own computer, and nothing you do on the server does it for them. Ask whether they still want it.

Installing one is a config change to a single file: .grizzly/env, at the top of the server's data directory. It is always there, sometimes empty — read_file it first to see what's already installed, then change it like any other config file, and the restart that applies it self-guards the same way. Only five keys in it do anything and the rest are ignored: TYPE (FABRIC to run mods; datapacks work on plain VANILLA), VERSION (the Minecraft version), MODRINTH_PROJECTS (the comma-separated list of slugs, a datapack written as datapack:slug), MODRINTH_DOWNLOAD_DEPENDENCIES set to required so the libraries a mod needs come down with it, and MODRINTH_PROJECTS_DEFAULT_VERSION_TYPE for the rare project that only ships test builds. Two rules matter more than the rest. To remove something, rewrite MODRINTH_PROJECTS to the slugs that remain — never delete the line, because with the line gone nothing is reconciled and the mod stays installed while the file says otherwise. And write VERSION alongside the first MODRINTH_PROJECTS, set to the version you checked the mods against; never lower it later, because a world upgrades one way only. Before the first switch to FABRIC on a world that already has anything in it, take a backup_server first — putting a world back afterwards is something only an admin can do. After the restart, read_logs to confirm each mod really downloaded instead of assuming it did. Tell them up front that a first install takes a minute or so: it fetches the loader and every mod before the world even loads.

Good news — the fix took. The fresh boot log now shows `[init] Setting initial memory to 2G and max to 2G` and the server is proceeding past the point where it was dying.

Here's a summary of what happened:

**The problem:** When the memory setting was tweaked, `MEMORY=96M` got written into the server's environment file. That sets the Java heap (initial *and* max) to 96 megabytes — nowhere near enough to boot a Minecraft server, so Java threw `OutOfMemoryError` every single time it started, even before the world loaded.

**The fix:** I changed `MEMORY=96M` to `MEMORY=2G` in `.grizzly/env` and restarted. The server has plenty of headroom (its container allows up to 4 GiB), so 2G is a comfortable, safe value for your Fabric setup with lithium, chunky, and krypton.

The previous version of the file is saved, so if you ever want to roll that back, it's one command. I've also got a watch on the startup — once the server finishes booting I'll confirm it's fully healthy with no out-of-memory errors.
